props.title: Blood on Satan's Claw

sections.content: Blood on Satan's Claw stands as a defining piece of British folk horror, alongside Witchfinder General (1968) and The Wicker Man (1973). Director Piers Haggard crafts a deeply unsettling tale of demonic possession in 17th century England, where children begin growing patches of fur and falling under satanic influence. The film's atmospheric dread and unflinching violence marked a significant shift from Hammer Horror's Gothic romanticism toward a more visceral, earthier brand of horror that would influence films like A Field in England (2013) and Kill List (2011).

sections.content: The film's depiction of corrupted youth and pagan ritual violence established key folk horror tropes that echo through modern works like Midsommar (2019) and The Ritual (2017). Its portrayal of demonic influence spreading through a rural community like a disease was revolutionary for its time, predating similar themes in Children of the Corn (1984) and The Village (2004).

What sets Blood on Satan's Claw apart is its unflinching approach to period detail and religious hysteria. Unlike the more fantastical Hammer productions of the era, the film grounds its horror in authentic 17th century agricultural life. This attention to historical accuracy would later influence films like The VVitch (2015) and Apostle (2018), where isolation and period-specific religious beliefs fuel the horror. sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in the recent folk horror renaissance, particularly in works like In the Earth (2021) and Men (2022). Its emphasis on landscape as a character - with evil literally emerging from the soil - established a template for how rural settings could become active participants in horror narratives. This approach is evident in modern folk horror films like Lamb (2021) and Gaia (2021).
